..(Sunday through Friday)
Issued at 415 PM EDT FRI JUL 24 2026

The long term forecast will be dominated by upper level ridging 
centered over the Great Plains, with troughing along the East Coast. 
Eastern Kentucky will find itself sandwiched between these features, 
leading to an extensive period of northwesterly flow aloft. A series 
of shortwaves will traverse this flow, providing a chance for 
multiple rounds of showers and storms (potentially in the form of 
MCS activity). However, confidence in the timing or intensity of 
these impulses remains low, and impacts to the forecast area will 
remain heavily dependent on the evolution of upstream convection, 
increasing uncertainty.

On Sunday, increasingly northwesterly winds will work to pull in 
better quality moisture from the Midwest, allowing dewpoints to 
climb into the upper 60s and low 70s across the forecast area by 
Sunday afternoon. Concurrently, mostly clear skies and increasing 
influence of the upper level ridge aloft will allow temperatures to 
rise into the mid 80s across the forecast area, allowing for 
moderate instability to build, although in the absence of forcing to 
drive convective initiation, rain chances will likely be relegated 
to an isolated storm or two at most through the daytime hours, if 
that. Some models are attempting to hint at isolated to perhaps 
widely scattered storm chances in our southernmost counties on 
Sunday afternoon, and the thermodynamic environment will certainly 
be capable of supporting convection. That being said, many models 
depict height rises at the same time, corresponding with a modest 
eastward expansion of the ridge aloft, which would inhibit 
convection. For now, NBM PoPs were retained, keeping rain chances 
below 10% across the forecast area through the evening.

Forecast uncertainty increases overnight Sunday into Monday as 
convective coverage increases in the Midwest, with some model 
guidance suggesting MCS type activity may approach the forecast area 
as soon as very early Monday morning. That being said, the most 
favored outcome at this time is that skies remain relatively clear, 
owing to surface high pressure lingering on the periphery of the 
forecast area. For now, a modest ridge/valley temperature split was 
introduced on Sunday night, in addition to typical valley fog, to 
account for this more likely solution.

Monday and Tuesday appear to offer the most robust storm chances of 
the period, with additional impulses moving through northwest flow 
aloft and a continued signal for MCS activity somewhere in the Ohio 
Valley. Although there is limited agreement in the timing or 
intensity of these waves, machine learning guidance has generally 
highlighted a broad area of severe potential from the Midwest into 
the Ohio Valley early next week, largely driven by the potential for 
damaging wind gusts associated with any convective complexes. This 
risk remains highly uncertain, and the current SPC Day 4 and 5 15% 
contours do not currently include our area (with Mondays risk area 
north of Kentucky in the Great Lakes region and Tuesdays risk more 
focused on the Mid Atlantic). That being said, the modeled 
environment does seem to support the potential for MCS activity to 
propagate southeast into the forecast area, and should diurnal 
timing of these waves also be favorable, the parameter space will be 
capable of supporting strong to severe storms. LREF mean surface 
based CAPE is in the range of 1500-2000 J/kg on Monday and Tuesday 
evening, and LREF mean 0-6 km shear is again in the neighborhood of 
30-40 kts, enough to support severe weather. Depending on how many 
rounds of showers and storms we receive, flash flooding could also 
potentially be a concern, although this remains similarly uncertain; 
the Weather Prediction Center has assigned a Marginal (Level 1/4) 
Risk for Excessive Rainfall on both Monday and Tuesday to account 
for this possibility. In short, there will be multiple chances for 
rain early next week, and upstream convective evolution, in addition 
to wave timing, will dictate impacts to the forecast area. 

Following potential activity on Tuesday into early Wednesday, rain 
chances will decrease again as moisture declines courtesy of 
increasingly northerly to northeasterly winds. High temperatures 
will generally rise into the upper 80s each day, with surface high 
pressure building in the vicinity of OH/WV.
